title: Authorize deployment service roles and editors without long-lived lab keys
description:
PLANNING ONLY. Ryan requested filing and design before implementation. This issue is not authorization to build runtime features, deploy, change cloud permissions, publish packages, push, or migrate production data. Keep open pending design review and separate implementation authorization.

As a account administrator, I want scoped deployment and human access to remote outputs, so that sites share the lab without exposing other tenants or durable credentials.

Feature: Scoped remote lab access
  Scenario: A deployment requests its configured outputs
    Given a deployment service role authorized for a reviewed publication/output scope
    When it authenticates to the remote lab using the approved mechanism
    Then it can request only the permitted decisions and history
    And it does not require a long-lived shared lab key
  Scenario: Unauthorized cross-publication feedback
    Given a deployment or editor lacks permission for another publication's output
    When it attempts to read restricted history or submit a label or steering command
    Then access is denied without changing labels, learning or classifier configuration
  Scenario: Expired or revoked authority
    Given a role or human session is expired or revoked
    When it attempts a lab operation
    Then the request fails explicitly without falling back to a broader identity

Design review / future Definition of Done: review these observable acceptance cases with the shared contract; executable specs and implementation are future work after authorization.
Open: account/tenant boundary, actor attribution, token exchange/federation/service-role mechanism, expiry/revocation and read/review/steer/admin capabilities. This is not authorization to create IAM roles, keys or cloud policy.

Preserve optional curated-example priming (decision-flywheel-da886c09-7acb-45d3-acf8-c81585f26d8a), its preview/revision/explicit-label acceptance contract, and separate existing scholarly research-paper and web-summary transformations. Priming must never become an onboarding gate. Common input items are distinct from publication-specific decisions; one publication accepting an item must never implicitly label another output.
